1:
Henry reads the opening as a caution against all fellowship with idols and idolaters: those taken into communion with God must have no communication with the unfruitful works of darkness. Bloody work is here appointed them, and yet it is God's work, and in its time and place needful and honourable. God engages first to do his part: it is taken for granted that he would bring them into the land of promise and cast out the nations then occupying it — his power is irresistible, and therefore he can do it; his promise is inviolable, and therefore he will. The nations are named and numbered, seven in all, and seven to one is great odds; they are specified that Israel might know the bounds of their commission, for hitherto their severity must come and no further. Henry presses that limit hard. The confining of the commission to the nations here mentioned plainly intimates that after-ages were not to draw this into a precedent, and it will not serve to justify those barbarous laws which give no quarter; however agreeable the method was to a dispensation in which beasts were killed and burnt in sacrifice, now that all sacrifices of atonement are superseded by the great propitiation, human blood has become more precious than it was, and those who have most power must not be prodigal of it.

The nations are owned to be greater and mightier than Israel, and Henry finds an argument in that too: they had long been rooted in the land to which Israel came strangers, and had men more expert in war, yet none of this shall prevent their being cast out — the strength of Israel's enemies magnifies the power of Israel's God. Then Israel must do their part: if God casts the nations out, Israel must not take them in, not as tenants, nor tributaries, nor servants. Henry gives two reasons for the severity: punishment for the wickedness they and their fathers had been guilty of, the iniquity of the Amorites being now full; and prevention of the mischief they would do if left alive, since the people of these abominations must not be mingled with the holy seed — better that these lives should be lost from the earth than that the true worship of God should be lost in Israel. So, he adds, we must deal with the lusts that war against our souls, which God has delivered into our hands by the promise that sin shall not have dominion over us: let us make no covenants with them, but mortify and crucify them.

On the number itself the commentators differ a little. Clarke observes that in several places of the Hebrew text the seven are not all enumerated, one or another being left out, which the Greek generally supplies; and he opens the chapter by laying out its argument — no covenant with the seven nations, no matrimonial alliances lest they be enticed into idolatry, all monuments of idolatry destroyed, and Israel a holy people made such not for its merits but for God's mercies. Wesley notices that ten nations were named to Abraham where seven are named here, and supposes that in the hundreds of years between, three were either destroyed by wars or swallowed up in the rest by cohabitation and marriage. Ellicott sets the chapter in the structure of the book: the former chapter applies the decalogue to the love of Jehovah and may be regarded as an expansion of the first commandment, while the exhortation here concerns the treatment of idolaters in the conquest and the avoidance of any union with them that might turn Israel from Jehovah — which connects with the first commandment and the second alike. Gill notes only that the introduction into the land is here ascribed not to Israel or their leaders but to the Lord as their covenant God.
2:
Calvin meets the charge of cruelty in this command, and answers that those who make it usurp too great authority over him who is the judge of all. The objection is specious that the people of God were imbued with inhumanity, sparing neither sex nor age. But when God had destined the land for his people, he was at liberty to destroy the former inhabitants; and beyond that, he desired the just demonstration of his vengeance to appear upon these nations. Four hundred years before he had suspended his sentence and borne with them if haply they might repent — that well-known saying, that the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full. After mercy shown for four centuries, and clemency that only increased their audacity, it was no cruelty to compensate for the delay by the grievousness of the punishment. Hence the perversity of the human intellect: we are indignant if he does not smite at once, yet when he comes forth as the avenger of guilt we call him cruel. It is said elsewhere that the land spewed them out, as if easing itself of a burden; and if impiety is intolerable to the lifeless element, why wonder that God exercised extreme severity? If his wrath was just he might choose what executioners he pleased, and having given this commission it was not unreasonable to forbid them to pity those he had appointed for destruction — for what is more preposterous than for servants to show mercy when it pleases the Master to be severe?

Ellicott is careful about the order of the clauses, and would divide them so that the destruction follows the smiting: when the Lord shall have delivered the nations, and thou hast smitten them, then thou shalt utterly destroy them, making them a devoted thing. In any case Jehovah's deliverance of the nations is to precede their defeat, so that indiscriminate attack and massacre are not to be thought of: all the operations described in Joshua were undertaken under divine direction, as were the battles of Moses's lifetime and of the judges. If Israelites and idolaters were united there was an end to the distinction of race and religion, and to the isolation of the people of Jehovah as exhibiting his law to mankind. But the isolation here commanded was only a means to an end and not the end itself: when the religious principles of the nation were sufficiently fixed to make their political supremacy unnecessary, that supremacy was taken away.

On the marriages they all limit the prohibition to the unconverted. Gill notes that it did not hold where the stranger became a proselyte, instancing Rahab and Ruth the Moabitess; otherwise it was unlawful, and bad consequences followed, as in the case of Solomon. Wesley reasons from the stated ground, that there is manifest danger of apostasy from such matches, which both limits the law to the unconverted and extends it beyond these seven to other idolatrous nations. Clarke puts the danger shortly: the heart being naturally inclined to evil, the idolatrous wife is likelier to draw aside the believing husband than he to bring her over. On the monuments Ellicott observes that such a course must bring matters to a crisis, since the inhabitants would either rise in defence of the objects of their worship, which would end in their extermination, or adopt the worship of Jehovah; the word rendered groves means here the grove in which the idol was worshipped, though sometimes it is used of the image, and David treated the images of the Philistines in just this way. Wesley says God designed to take away whatever might bring their idolatry to remembrance; Keil, that Israel was bound to destroy them by virtue of their election as a holy people; and Clarke, that the nations must either embrace the true religion or be cut off.
6:
Calvin takes the fewness of the people as the very illustration of grace. He declares first the end of their election, that God bestowed this honour on them in order to acquire a holy people, pure from all pollutions; whence we gather that in proportion to the grace with which anyone is endued he is bound to live piously, for God does not wish his gifts to lie idle, and when he adopts us into his Church we are called not to uncleanness but to purity of life. The Hebrew word rendered special some understand of a treasure, gold and pearls being designated by it elsewhere; but it is agreed that the title is given the elect people because God delights himself in them, and herein his goodness shines forth, that he so highly esteems such worthless creatures. Clarke notes that the Greek renders it a peculiar people, a private property, and that Peter quotes it in that form. Ellicott presses the phrase before it: not merely a holy nation, as in Exodus, but a holy people, a state whose very constitution was holiness to Jehovah — and such a state could tolerate nothing displeasing to him.

On the reason for the choice, Calvin observes that an equal distribution of God's gifts casts obscurity on them in our eyes — the sun and our common food lose their value — while what is peculiar is more conspicuous. Moses takes it for granted that there was nothing in the people to make their condition better than another's, and infers that God had no reason for choosing them but his mere choice. And the love is referred back from the children to the fathers, God not having begun to love this generation for the first time — so that they are his peculiar people by right of inheritance, and even in Abraham's case God was induced to be kind by no cause but mere generosity. Ellicott adds the observable fact: the Moabites, Ammonites, Ishmaelites and Edomites, all like Israel descended from Terah, developed far faster than the chosen line — Abraham had twelve grandsons through Ishmael but only as many great-grandsons through Isaac and Jacob, and kings reigned in Edom before any reigned over Israel. Keil says the honour rested on the word given at Sinai, that Jehovah bound himself to them in love, not for their multitude, but though they were the least of nations.

The description of God that follows Calvin treats as borrowed from the second commandment and inserted here in confirmation of the whole law. Of the harder clause Calvin rejects two readings — that God confers kindnesses on the wicked only to destroy them at last, and that he repays them in his anger — and interprets it of the face of those whose arrogance God humbles: their brazen front shall avail nothing, and they shall as certainly feel the judgment they despise as if it were set before their eyes. God does not deal with the wicked as with his children, so that what is medicine to believers is to the reprobate a foretaste of eternal destruction. As for the swiftness of the vengeance, which seems not to accord with the passages that call God slow to anger, a thousand years in his sight are but a day, so that when we think he delays he is hastening as much as is necessary. Wesley reads those that hate him widely, not only of such as hate him directly, but of those who oppose his people and his word; and to their face as openly, so that they shall see it and not avoid it. Gill records the Targums' reading, in their lifetime, and offers the alternative that it is God's face, of impudent sinners like those of Sodom. Keil calls this energy of the covenant God's grace and holiness a powerful admonition to keep his commandments.
12:
Henry says the promise of God's favour is enlarged upon with an affecting copiousness which intimates how much it is both God's desire and our own interest that we be religious. If they would sincerely do their part of the covenant, God would certainly perform his: let us be constant in our duty, and we cannot question the constancy of his mercy. If they would love God and devote themselves to him, he would love them and bless them and multiply them greatly. He began in love to us, and if we return his love in filial duty then, and only then, may we expect its continuance. The increase of their families and of their stock alike is promised, so that they should have neither estates without heirs nor heirs without estates. And if they kept themselves pure from the idolatries of Egypt, God would keep them clear from its diseases — for diseases are God's servants, which go where he sends them, so that it is good for the health of our bodies to mortify the sin of our souls. Their duty would itself be their advantage: they shall consume the nations, which is the precept, and God shall destroy them, which is the promise — as we are told not to let sin reign, and promised that it shall not have dominion.

Calvin faces the conditional form of the words. God appears so to act by agreement as to leave his people no hope of favour unless they perform their part, this being the usual form in the law, where the condition is inserted that God will do good if they have deserved it. Still, after God has so covenanted, he descends to the gratuitous promise of pardon, reconciling the unworthy to himself; the original covenant avails only to man's condemnation, but when salvation is offered gratuitously their works become pleasing to God. All calculation of merit is out of the question; yet God deals with them as if they did something to deserve it. Wesley reads the promise as the covenant of mercy, which God of his mere grace made with them. Clarke draws the opposite inference: their continuance in favour was to depend on their faithfulness to God's grace, and if they rebelled, though he had chosen them through love, he would cast them off in justice — the elect may become unfaithful and so reprobates, as happened to those whose carcasses fell in the wilderness.

On the diseases Calvin asks whether Moses means the boils generated by the scattered ashes, or the lice, or maladies prevailing long before the departure. He inclines to the last, since a later chapter, after the botch of Egypt, adds emerods and the scab and the itch — so that Israel should be free by privilege from various Egyptian diseases if only they obeyed. Ellicott notes that the word for diseases occurs only in this book, and that the law of Moses was in many details a sanitary quite as much as a moral code, the root pointing to the languors that arise from violating God's laws, moral and physical alike. Keil traces the blessing to God's love, particularised on the fruit of the body, the fruits of the soil and the rearing of cattle; the word for the flocks' increase he thinks a Canaanite term from Astarte. On the command to consume the nations Ellicott observes that when delivered to Israel they are delivered for execution, the time being in Jehovah's hand; and Calvin, that God's design was not only to punish but to have the land where his name was to be invoked purged from all pollutions, since any survivors would soon have revived their corruptions, and Israel, disposed enough to superstition already, would easily have been drawn to idols. Gill notes that the sickness to be taken away is bodily, whether prevented or removed when come.
17:
Calvin makes the anticipated misgiving an occasion of doctrine. Since it was a matter of great difficulty to destroy such a multitude, God anticipates the people's fear and exhorts them to the strenuous execution of his sentence; and from this we gather a useful instruction, that whenever God commands anything which exceeds our power we must still obey, and boldly break through whatever obstacles impede us. In all arduous matters let this come to our aid, that whatever is contrary to God's will may easily be annihilated by his almighty power. But since terror so lays hold of all our senses that we lie as it were torpid, God recalls what abundant grounds of confidence he had supplied: all the miracles he had wrought were proofs of his invincible power, whence they should conclude that nothing was to be dreaded so long as God went before them, and that, assured of victory, they should not descend to any treaties. Gill notes that the misgivings are secret thoughts of the heart, inwardly retained though not outwardly expressed.

Ellicott finds the appeal to Egypt exactly weighted. No free nation could have the same ground for terror as a nation of slaves rising against its masters; and if Israel had been delivered by Jehovah in that position, it was a security for all time that he would give them the victory in every enterprise he called them to. On the word rendered temptations he observes that the repeated summonses to Pharaoh, enforced by plagues, may well be called temptations in the sense of trials of his character, since the word in the sense of inducement to sin is very rare, if not wanting, in the Old Testament. Wesley reads the word of Israel rather than of Pharaoh, as the trials of their faith and obedience. Keil says simply that Israel had no need to be afraid, since Jehovah was in the midst of them a mighty God and terrible, who would smite the nations with great confusion till they were destroyed — as at Gibeon — and deliver their kings into Israel's hand, so that their names should vanish from under heaven. Gill takes the fear deprecated to be of their numbers and gigantic stature alike.

On the hornet Calvin explains why a second instrument was needed. The destruction of their enemies might seem long if they were only to be slain by Israelite weapons, and it was scarcely credible that men would voluntarily stretch out their own throats; so, lest the Israelites be alarmed at imagining their enemies vigorous in resistance, God declares that other forces should be at hand, and that hornets or other poisonous insects should destroy the fugitives. The same declaration stands in Exodus, and Joshua relates that what God promised he performed. But since these nations were not to be destroyed in a moment, lest the people grow weary, God reminds them that the delay would be to their advantage: if all the inhabitants were exterminated at once the wild beasts would occupy the empty land, so that the prolonging of the war was itself a provision for the people's welfare. Calvin adds that though a similar promise stands in Exodus he places this under another head, because the object here is that none of the ancient pollutions should remain in the land, and that Israel should not mingle with the ungodly, by whose arts they might be drawn away to spurious religions. Ellicott would take the hornet literally, remarking that a land flowing with milk and honey may well have swarmed with bees and hornets; Gill understands not one but several, creatures resembling wasps though twice as large, and records that Aben Ezra interpreted the word of the leprosy. Keil notes that God had already promised the hornets in Exodus, and that they should pursue until all who were left and had hidden themselves had perished.
22:
Clarke gives the plain reason for the gradual expulsion: Israel was not yet numerous enough to fill the whole land, and since wild animals multiply where a place is thinly peopled, God tells them that though they might expel the nations at once by force of arms, it would be impolitic, lest the beasts of the field multiply upon them. Ellicott illustrates the verb rendered put out from its other uses — of the axe-head flying off the handle in mid-blow, and of the olive casting its fruit — and takes by little and little as confirming that each nation's expulsion was contingent on the divine decree, none being attacked except when the Lord should deliver them up. Gill observes that the gradualness is mentioned for their encouragement, since seeing that all were not destroyed at once they might fear the work would never be accomplished. Ellicott adds that in the summary of Joshua's conquest the kings are reckoned for the cities, and that the promise about none being able to stand was renewed personally to Joshua; Gill counts one and thirty of them, and Wesley notes that the promise is conditional on their performing their duty, which they neglecting, they justly lost the benefit of it.

On the images Calvin observes that the command goes further than before. Having forbidden them to worship the gods of the land, God now commands them to burn the graven images, since the people were prone to superstition and such snares might easily have alienated them from his pure worship; and he does not merely bid them melt the gold and silver, but altogether interdicts its use. He shows thereby how greatly God abominates idols, since whoever touched the materials of which they were molten would contract pollution and become accursed. This severity might seem to condemn the metals, created for man's use, as if natural things could be corrupted by man — for in that way idolaters would contaminate the sun and moon when they falsely made them objects of worship. The answer is that the gold and silver were not polluted by this impious abuse, but that, free from stain in themselves, they were polluted in respect to the people. Such was the uncleanness of animals, which had no pollution in themselves but which God had interdicted for food; otherwise the ignorant people could not be restrained, and so God would have that be abominable which in itself was pure. Still this was a political precept, given only temporarily to that ancient people; yet we gather from it how detestable idolatry is, which infects even the works of God with its filthiness.

The others take the prohibition more practically. Clarke supposes that some of the ancient idols were plated with gold, and that God saw the value of the metal and the excellence of the workmanship might tempt Israel to preserve them, which could lead, remotely at least, to idolatry — and as the idols were accursed, so were all who had them. Keil agrees that the danger was not chiefly that they should practise idolatry with the metal, but that silver and gold used in idolatrous worship was an abomination to Jehovah, not to be brought into their houses lest they fall under the ban to which all objects of idolatry were devoted — as the history of Achan proves; such a thing was to be destroyed by burning or grinding to powder. Gill extends the abomination beyond the metal to the idol itself and its utensils, this care being taken to prevent all appearance of idolatry; and he presses the curse, since if it enters the house of the thief or the perjurer, much more the house of an idolater. Wesley says the command covers not only the silver or gold on the idols but their other ornaments, and was given to show God's utter detestation of idolatry.
